title: ask — the bridge's transport envelope. It carries; it does not author (4.4).
description: An envelope asserts three things and creates none of them: this is the card the other side sent, this is what the gates said about it, and this is the round it belongs to. Each gate has three outcomes rather than two -- it passed, it failed, or the tables do not say -- because a boolean forces the bridge to claim it knows something a skeleton table cannot tell it, and inventing that is the one thing 4.4 forbids. A failed gate produces a refusal card instead of an envelope; a gate that cannot be resolved holds the round and gives the turn to a person.

thread.description: a solo- thread has no bridge round in it by definition (5.2)

round.description: round 0 means no bridge round is involved, so it cannot be an envelope

status.description: the bridge executes nothing, so an envelope never reaches APPROVED, RUNNING or DONE. VALIDATED means wrapped and gated, which is not the same as actionable: whether the other side may act is in the thread ledger's turn, not here.

numbers.description: the bridge authors no numbers. The payload's numbers stay in the payload where they keep their own sources and grades; copying them up here would re-declare them, and a re-declared grade is a laundered grade (5.3, check 21).

payload_card.description: the plan or result card, carried without a character changed

answerability.description: can the other side produce this observable at all? Refuse before spending a round (4.4 rule 3). The verdict is derived from contracts/observables.json and the other side's capabilities table, never declared here: the validator recomputes it and rejects a card that claims more than the tables say.

producible.description: yes: a configuration in that table produces it. no: the vocabulary or a populated table says that side cannot, and then this must be a refusal card rather than an envelope. undeclared: the table has not declared it, which is not the same as impossible -- the round is held and a person names the observable first.

producing_configs.description: required when producible is yes: which configurations of the receiving side produce it

substitutes.description: observables the other side does declare, taken from its capabilities table. Attached to a no so the refusal carries somewhere to go (4.4 failure table).

unit_consistency.description: the bridge checks; it does not convert (4.4 rule 2, 5.7). Reduced units never appear in a card, so there is no mapping to apply.

verdict.description: no_counterpart is the opening round: there is nothing on the other side to compare against yet. From round two on it means the comparison was skipped, which is a failure.

compared_against.description: id of the counterpart card the units were compared with; null only with no_counterpart

trigger.description: What opened this round. The bridge never opens one itself (4.4), so these two are the whole list. `plan_completion` is the plan card reaching its finished state -- validated, past DRAFT -- and not a run finishing: a completed plan is what tells the other side what to measure, and a plan crossing is the normal opening of a thread. `human` is a person handing a card over, and it is the only way a result crosses, because a finished run opening a round by itself would be a second automatic trigger and 4.4 grants one. Note what this does not mean: a plan crossing is not a comparison. M4's condition is two results measured for the same observable, and that needs a run on each side; carrying a plan is how the second side learns which run to do.

value_comparison.description: The third gate, and the only one that compares two VALUES. Answerability asks whether the other side can produce the observable at all and unit_consistency asks whether the two sides mean the same units; neither looks at what the numbers say. From round two on there is a counterpart, and putting a measurement beside a model is what this agent is for (4.4).

verdict.description: tie means the two values are inside P15's band (5.8), differs means outside it, no_counterpart means the opening round has nothing to compare against.

grade.description: Required on a tie and derived, never chosen: it is the WORSE of the two values compared (5.8.1). A computed value inherits the worst input in its chain and so does the verdict of a comparison -- no new threshold, the rule 5.8 already had, applied to comparison. A tie between E2 and E5 is an E5 tie, and it is the UNGRADED tie that misleads: 'no disagreement at E5' reads correctly where 'no disagreement' alone reads as agreement. Check 63 recomputes it from the two operands and refuses a card that claims better, the way check 8 recomputes answerability -- a verdict the writer can choose is not a gate.

of.description: The two numbers compared, by the card that carries each and its name in that card's numbers[]. The grades are not repeated here: they live on those numbers, and a copy beside them is a second place to be wrong (11-11).

card.description: the id of the card carrying the number

number.description: its name in that card's numbers[]

supersedes.description: The round this one replaces, when the source card moved to a new revision under it (4.4 rule 5). A repeat re-asks what was answered; a superseding round asks the same question of a source that changed, and nothing was answered. NOT a claim: check 8 recomputes it from the two rounds' ledgers, which already record the source revision, and refuses a round that says it supersedes one whose revision did not move. Conditions are deliberately not in the duplicate key -- that would let a writer open a second round by nudging one number, which is a verdict the writer chooses. Naming the superseded round and having the ledgers corroborate it cannot be faked.
